notes.shape: A yield curve graphs Treasury yields across maturities from 1 month to 30 years; an upward slope indicates longer-term bonds yield more than short-term, reflecting normal economic expectations. An inverted curve, where shorter-term yields exceed longer-term yields, has historically preceded every modern US recession by 6 to 18 months. Currently, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.71% (due June 2026), and the 10Y-2Y spread is 0.36 percentage points, indicating a positively sloped yield curve. This marks a recovery from the 2022-2024 period when the curve was inverted at or below 0.0 points, reflecting an unusual and recession-warning downward slope.
notes.signal: The 2s10s spread, the difference between 10-year and 2-year Treasury yields, acts as a reliable recession indicator; inversion (spread <= 0) typically signals recession risk. The series experienced its deepest inversion at 0.0 points during 2022-2024 but has since re-steepened above zero to 0.36 points, implying a normalization. However, the yield curve often un-inverts shortly before a recession, so a positive slope does not rule out near-term economic downturns. Complementing this, the NY Fed recession probability remains elevated at 31%, suggesting moderate ongoing recession risks despite the current positive spread.
notes.now: The yield curve's positive slope of 0.36 points after a recent inversion and the 4.71% 10-year yield reflect an easing of immediate recession signals. Nonetheless, the 31% probability of recession from the NY Fed indicates that economic headwinds persist. Together, these metrics suggest cautious vigilance without definitive closure on recession risk or timing.
